history.insight: Horizontally partitions a database into smaller, faster pieces called shards across multiple database servers to overcome single-machine storage and throughput limits.
Decouples producers from consumers, provides backpressure buffering, and ensures asynchronous processing and horizontal scalability under heavy traffic spikes.
Distributes keys across nodes using a hash ring. When nodes are added or removed, only k/n keys need remapping on average, minimizing cache churn in distributed caches.
In a distributed system experiencing a network partition (P), you can guarantee either Consistency (C) or Availability (A), but never both simultaneously.
An extension of Dijkstra's algorithm that uses heuristics (f(n) = g(n) + h(n)) to intelligently guide graph search toward the goal with optimal paths.
Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm searches for occurrences of a word within a main text in O(n + m) time using a precomputed longest prefix-suffix (LPS) array.
Maintains elements in strictly increasing or decreasing order. Essential for solving 'Next Greater Element' and largest rectangle in histogram in O(n).
Uses two references to traverse an array or string from opposite ends or at varying speeds, reducing quadratic O(n^2) search spaces to linear O(n).
A complete binary tree satisfying the heap property. Min-heaps allow O(1) peek, O(log n) insert and extraction, fundamental for Dijkstra and heap sort.
Produces a linear ordering of vertices in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge (u, v), vertex u comes before v. Solved using Kahn's algorithm (indegree) or DFS.
Combines a doubly linked list with a hash map to achieve O(1) get and put operations while maintaining access order for eviction.
Also known as the Tortoise and Hare algorithm, uses two pointers moving at different speeds (1 step and 2 steps) to detect cycles in linked lists in O(n) time and O(1) space.
DSU or Union-Find tracks elements partitioned into disjoint subsets. With path compression and union by rank, operations run in nearly O(1) amortized time (inverse Ackermann function α(n)).
Solves complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems with optimal substructure. Memoization (top-down) and tabulation (bottom-up) eliminate redundant computation.
A tree data structure for storing intervals or segments, allowing querying range sum/min/max and point/range updates in O(log n) time.
Divides the search interval in half repeatedly on sorted collections, running in logarithmic time O(log n). Always watch out for integer overflow: use mid = low + (high - low) // 2.
A tree-like data structure used for efficient retrieval of keys in a dataset of strings, ideal for autocomplete and spell-checkers with O(L) lookup where L is word length.
Finds the single-source shortest path in weighted graphs with non-negative edges using a min-heap in O((V + E) log V) time.
Hash maps achieve average O(1) time complexity by mapping keys to bucket indices using a hash function. Collision resolution commonly uses chaining or open addressing (linear/quadratic probing).
